observation.visible_scene: A male mandarin duck perched on a mossy stone at the edge of a shallow, flowing stream; blurred green mossy banks and moving water fill the background. The duck remains seated throughout, its body oriented away from the camera with the head turned back over its own flank.
visible_changes: The duck's head and neck cycle through a preening motion: in the early frames the bill is tucked toward the upper wing/back, then the head lifts and rotates (frames ~10-12), then it tucks back into the shoulder and breast area for the remainder of the clip, with brief motion-blurred head turns (frames ~20-22).
The two upright orange 'sail' feathers shift angle and position as the torso twists, sometimes standing more erect and sometimes leaning, rather than translating across the frame.
The blue-green crest feathers on the head flare and change apparent length as the head rotates, becoming more prominent in the later half of the clip.
The water surface shows continuous ripples and shifting bright reflections, indicating flowing stream motion independent of the duck.
The duck's body and feet stay fixed on the stone; the mossy rocks in the background keep their positions, so the framing is essentially static while only the bird's head/neck and the water move.
outside_clip_unknowns: What preceded the clip (e.g., whether the duck had just finished bathing or feeding) and what it does after the segment ends are not shown.
The exact feather tracts the bill is working on at each moment are partly hidden by the bird's own body.
uncertain_details: Any very small handheld camera drift is hard to confirm because the background rocks stay largely in place; the dominant visible motion is the duck's own head/neck movement and the water flow.
Whether the orange sail-feather changes are pure deformation/rotation of the feathers or partly occlusion by the moving wing is not fully resolvable from the frames.
